Any creatures played this way gain update is actually very simple. Only two words are added to the rules text, but this change strengthens a number of decks, especially in the Modern format. These two words—"you can. " The final part of the description of "Exile" now reads as follows. When the last time counter is removed, you may play this card without paying its mana cost. While this change is incredibly small, it affects two of the strongest decks in Modern: Mono-Red Bern and Four-Color Rhino. Both of these powerful cards with the Exile mechanic , so let's take a look at how exactly they were affected. For the Rhinos, the usual game plan is to simply the cascade to play the key card "Rumble of Footsteps " and put the Rhinos onto the battlefield on turn three. But sometimes you just have a copy of this card in your starting hand and just "banish" it on the first turn. Since Rhinos are a very popular deck, one of the sideboard cards against them is Raging Whirlwind. This is a two-mana red enchantment that has the following ability: " Whenever a player casts a spell without spending mana, Raging Whirlwind deals damage to that player." " Storming Whirlwind" is great against incarnations and obtained through cascade. Of course, in both of these cases, you could simply not the spell to avoid taking five points of damage. However, with cards that have Exile, you never had that choice. The Banishment rule read: " When the last time counter is removed, cast it without paying its mana cost." In the middle of the game, if a player used a deck to pause Rift Bolt, and their opponent Leyline of Sanctity on their turn with no creatures on the field, then when the turn returned to the player with Rift Bolt, they had no choice but to direct the spell at themselves or one of their creatures. Commander currently has around 1,900 legendary creatures, planeswalkers or that can be your commander, and around 26,000 cards allowed for use in your deck. To me, that's quite a large selection, and it seems a bit overwhelming. So in today's video, I'll help you narrow down your choices by telling you how to find your next favorite commander , what themes to choose for inspiration, and giving you some tips on etiquette when playing at your local gaming club. So, for those new to Commander, let 's do a quick overview of what it is . Commander is a 100-card format where you build a deck around a single legendary commander. You can only use colorless cards or cards of colors that commander's color identity. Your commander is in the command zone, and you can play him from there for his cost at any time you could play him from your hand. If you want to learn more about how to play Commander, check out this video at the link. The first step in choosing a commander is to understand what types of decks you like to build . Did you know that all decks throughout the history of Magic can be boiled down to four basic aggro, control, combo, and Let's take a look at them. Aggro decks, short for " aggressive," aim to end the game as quickly as possible. If you've played MTG Arena since launch, you've definitely encountered a aggressive deck in ranked games. If you don't get rid of their creatures and stabilize the game, it will end very quickly. A typical aggro deck in Commander is Muxus, Goblin Grandee or Krenko, Mob Boss. The game plan is simple. Deploy goblins , attack with them, and deal a lot of damage. If you're not a fan of mono-red, mono-green elves do the same thing, but a little more sophisticated. Look out for Marwyn , the Nurturer or Ezuri, Renegade Leader to lead the attack. So, while aggro decks want to win as quickly as possible, control decks are the complete opposite. They want to slow down the game, because they are true masters of card advantage. What control decks lack in creatures they more than number of cancellation and removal spells. Most control decks are mono-blue or blue combined with one or two other colors, but control decks can be played with other colors as well. Azami, Lady of the Scrolls—one of my favorite mono- blue control decks. These are actually " turn them over to draw cards, and win the game. Conveniently located between aggressive and decks are the called midrange decks. Midrange decks to control the early game with effective spells and then finish it off with powerful creatures. Almost all decks in Commander and all pre-made decks follow this style. Xenag, God of Rebellion, and Maren of Clan Nel both come to mind as midrange commanders. If you're looking for something newer, Aragorn, the definitely fits that style. Finally, our last main type of deck is combo decks. As the name suggests, combo decks aim to put together a combination and win the game on the spot. Combo decks in Commander are a controversial topic. You either love playing with them or you can't stand facing them. For example, Oracle of Tassa and Corrupted Pact are the most popular combination for instant victory. It only requires two cards and costs a total of four mana. Plus, you play colors that have the best card drawing, spell cancellation, and search capabilities. Personally, I don't mind combos existing in decks. I just don't like decks whose sole purpose is to find the same combination and just win the game. Of course, these are just the four deck archetypes. The key to victory in Commander is having a deck. Another approach to building a deck is to choose a specific theme that you like. I'll quickly talk about three of my favorite deck themes and the commanders that can be used in them . First , it's "Pillow Fort ." Pillow Fort decks are designed to make it difficult or completely stop attacks or damage from opponents as possible. This is an extremely defensive deck. My personal version, a full list of which can be found at moxfield.com, is led by Anna, Navigator of the Ship, a blue and white deck. This deck has a lot of spells , such as Phantom Prison, Propaganda, and Sphere of Safety, as well as creatures with abilities that prevent opponents from attacking. Blazing Archon, Windborn Muse, and even Peacekeeper—they're all great. Next we have Group Slug. So, one of the niche decks that people play are so- called group hug decks. These decks are designed to cards to everyone and mana acquisition. As the name suggests, group hugs share love. Group slug decks, on the other hand, punish anyone for any action, including yourself . My personal favorite is Nekusar, the Mindrazer , which specifically punishes players for taking cards. There is also Yarok, the Desecrated, who punishes players for excess mana. These decks love cards like Manabarbs, Spiteful Visions, or Spellshock. And speed up the game even more, maps like Descent into Avernus and Havoc Festival are a must. With the release of the new Lord of the Rings set, there are a lot of new commanders that I'm looking forward to building decks for. One of them is a spell deck with Lord of the Nazgûl as the commander. You can find Lord of the Nazgûl in the "Host of Mordor" prequel or, if you're lucky, in a set booster or collection booster . So, the game plan here is simple. Summon Lord of the Nazgûl , try to copy it with Spark Double or Sakashima the Impostor , then cast a bunch of cheap blue and black spells to create lots of ghosts and attack everyone at the table for the win. If you want to see a full deck breakdown on Lord of the Nazgûl, let me know in the comments below. With the release of Commander Masters on August 4, new players will join the game. So I think it's worth mentioning a few things to consider when sitting down to play Commander with newbies at your local gaming club. First, always keep in mind the power level of your deck. If you sit down to play with your Urza, Lord High Artificer deck and your opponents have just opened a precon, it's like arriving in a Formula 1 car at a go-kart track. You will definitely win the race, but neither you nor your opponents enjoy it. Personally, I like to have two different decks with me when I play Commander. My fan deck and my competitive deck. I just ask what decks people play, and nine times out of ten they will tell me how strong they think their deck is. Secondly, Commander is casual game. You only truly win the game when everyone at the table has had fun . If everyone was sitting around, unable to play because you were constantly other players' lands, or you just put together a two-card combo for an instant win without interacting with others in any way. Of course, you won. But is it really? And finally, accept the fact that in some games you will become the main enemy at the table, and three players will start attacking you or destroying your permanents. Maybe you've gained a big card advantage or started to build a multi-card combo . Commander is a format. In the end, there only be one winner. If players attack you, you're clearly doing something right, because everyone thinks you're about to win. So, that's it . A quick overview of the different types of Commander decks you can play with, and some tips to keep in mind when playing Commander at your local game store. What is your Commander deck or what advice would you give to a beginner? Let us know in the comments below. Thanks again to Wizards of the Coast for sponsoring this video, and thank you for watching. Have a good evening, see you next time.

full: Wizards just updated a card type that's almost 10 years old, and it significantly affects every format in the game. Let's talk about the rules update for Sagas in the Final Fantasy set. Judging by the Final Fantasy release notes, Wizards are going to change two Saga rules. Rule 714.3 B and rule 714.4. Let's start with rule 714.4. And we'll come back to the other change later. Rule 714.4 states that when a Saga has lore counters equal to or greater than the number of its chapters, and this is not a result of a chapter ability, the controller of that Saga sacrifices it as an action based on game state. This rule was used in Modern, where players sacrifice their Urza's Saga when Blood Moon was in play . The saga became a mountain and lost all chapter abilities, which means their number is zero. According to rule 714.2 D and current rule 714.4 , Saga should have been sacrificed. This decision was also important for future Saga creatures ( summons) from the Final Fantasy set. full: There was a recent rules change to sagas with the release of Secrets of Strixhaven, and I thought this change was a small nerve to sagas with read ahead. But oh boy, was I wrong, and it's so much worse than I thought. Not to mention, I had a bunch of people tell me that the rules have effectively changed nothing, but that's not the case. Let me explain. For some context, if you haven't already, I highly recommend you go and watch my previous video, linked in the corner here. Let's cover some things from that video. First, a bunch of people were saying that the main interaction I was talking about, Doubling Season interacting with sagas, has always worked that way, and this new rule changes nothing. For proof, I was cited the original Dominaria mechanics article written by Matt Tabak, a senior Magic editor and the former Magic rules manager. Where he says, "In some unusual cases, you might add more than one lore counter to a saga This can happen with effects like the one on Doubling Season. If The Flame of Keld enters the battlefield while you control Doubling Season, it will enter with two lore counters. This will cause the chapter one and two abilities to trigger, and you can actually put them on the stack in either order." He does then go on to say, and I think this is "The following turn, you'll add another lore counter. Note that Doubling Season won't affect this turn-based action." Matt Tabak also wrote the mechanics article for the Final Fantasy set that also happens to include Doubling Season interacting with sagas. "In some unusual cases, you may put more than one lore counter on a saga at a time. This can happen if you control a permanent like Doubling Season." And then there was the Brewer's Kitchen video that featured sagas and Doubling Season. And as you can see here, Doubling Season doubles the amount of token sagas, as well as having them enter with two counters. So, was I wrong here? Well, not this time. In a thread on Blue Sky, Matt does confirm that both the Dominaria and Final Fantasy articles were wrong, and that Doubling Season wouldn't interact with sagas, but because sagas entering with a counter was not an effect, nor was the turn-based action of adding a lore He goes on to clarify that Inkeeper's Talent or Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider are cards that can interact with sagas with the old rules. This is because those cards specifically care about counters being put on something, whereas Doubling Season only interacted with effects. So, what about Brewer's Kitchen's video? Well, I've done a video in the past pointing out that Arena doesn't get all of Magic's rules exactly right. Now, before the Arena haters come out of the woodwork, Arena gets the vast majority of the rules of the game correct. Otherwise, you'd see a whole lot more videos from myself reporting on the matter. Now, I wanted to clear up one small thing I did get wrong in my last video. So, to clarify, as of the release of Secrets of Strixhaven, it is no longer a straight rule that puts the initial counters on sagas, it's an intrinsic ability which creates a replacement effect. Because of this change, now Doubling Season will double the amount of counters a saga enters Doubling Season will continue not to interact with the turn-based action of putting a counter on a saga you control at the beginning of your first main Now, the bit that I did get wrong was with Read Ahead. In the video, I said when you played a saga with Read Ahead with Doubling Season in play, if you picked anything more than the first chapter, the saga would immediately end and the chapters would all trigger. That last part is incorrect. I was under the impression that the choice you made determined what chapters were skipped. When in actual fact, all it comes down to is the number of counters placed on the saga. So, if you decide you're going to read ahead to chapter two with Doubling Season in play, you'll go to put two counters on the saga. Doubling Season will see this and replace that with four counters. The saga enters with four counters and because there's no chapter four, the saga will be sacrificed as a state-based action and nothing else will happen. I want to clarify that this is specific to sagas with Read Ahead. For normal sagas and creature sagas, when they enter with more than one counter or have multiple counters placed on them, each chapter will trigger once and then you can stack them as you wish. Rule 714.2b covers this. Was there anything else you think I wasn't clear enough on and needed explaining again? Perhaps you'd like me to do a video on why you can't name anything when you cast Meddling Mage while there's a Humility in play. Let me know in the comments. As always, if you learned something, be sure to like this video and subscribe because if you don't, I'll get Wizards to change the rules for sagas again next year. Thanks for watching and I'll see you in the next one.

And while I used to attend these for all the awesome video games, this year I only had one thing on my mind, Magic the Gathering. And after that weekend, something was rekindled within me. For this year's packs, Magic was a big focus. Gavin Verhe, principal Magic the Gathering designer at Wizards of the Coast was giving the keynote speech and we also had American content creator Ben Baitman flown in. There was also a showcase of other Australian MTG talent, Good Games, Moley, Cozy Magic Club, After Hours, and Base Deck Department. On the Friday, I started packs off by learning to play the new League of Legends TCG Riftbound with none other than Instant Speed MTG Newsman, Toa MTG. It's a pretty interesting game and feels a lot like Commander. It's probably something I'll make a video about in the near future. Then later that evening, thanks to Gavin himself, I was invited to participate in Ben Baitman's Chaos Draft. Chaos Draft is where you take random boosters from Magic's history and draft with all of them. We had everything from Magic 30 to Homelands and Fallen Empires. We all gentlemans agreed that the winner of the draft would get to keep all of the cards we opened that night. Now, I did manage to draft an awesome red green aggro deck with Fireball and Overrun, but I'm really bad at social media and I didn't take any pictures of the deck. The deck did pretty well and the only loss I had that night was against Gavin who beat me with my own cards thanks to the black cat cunning thief that he drafted. So, while I didn't walk away with a stack of cards, I did have a lot of fun. On the Saturday, after designing some cards with Gavin, there was a porpa tournament. Porper, for those who don't know, is a 60c card format where the only cards you're allowed to play are commons. And after finding out that there was a Porper Tron deck, I quickly pulled one together and signed up. The goal of my deck was simple. Assemble Tron and then through the deck's multitudes of card draw, assemble the combo of Ashnod's Altar, two copies of Mer Retriever, and then either Pack Doll Terror for infinite damage or Golem Foundry for infinite creatures. I ended up going 211 in the tournament, only losing to my worst matchup in round one, a Mardu Synthesizer deck that was main decking cleansing wildfires. I'm so glad I played in this tournament. Thanks to this and the draft that I did on Friday, I realized how much I miss playing 1v1 60card formats. Standard has been absolutely soul draining, but playing porpa was so refreshing. You're probably going to see me talk a little bit more about porpa in the near future. I have no idea what that content looks like yet, but stay tuned. On Sunday, things were a lot more relaxed. I stopped over at the Cozy Magic Club meetup and scored some awesome sleeves from Palms Off Gaming, snuck in a quick game of Commander, and then headed off to Ben Baitman's panel about making a career for yourself in Magic the Gathering. Turns out the answer is post more content. Yeah, we'll see how that goes. There was an awesome PAX afterparty hosted at the Tessy Pearl, but because I'm bad at social media, I didn't take any pictures. But trust me, it was a lot of fun. A couple of dinners later, and that's my magic pack well and truly dusted. It's great to see that PAX had a focus on MTG this year. It personally feels like it was a real success. So, here's hoping it will be bigger and better next year. Have you ever been to PAX before? What do you think of the PAPA format? Let me know in the comments below. Thanks for watching and I'll see you in the next

We're talking about most of the mass sweeps: Wrath of God, Day of Judgment, Damnation, Chain Reaction, Blasphemous Act, Austere Command, and even the most hated card in Commander, Farewell. It also stops powerful cards like Force of Will, The Great Henge, Bolas's Citadel, Anointed Procession, Doubling Season, and Prismatic Bridge. And Haddock Teague stops not only them, but also some of the best combo finishers in the game. We're talking Finale of Devastation, Green Sun's Zenith, Chord of Calling, Exsanguinate, Storm King's Thunder, Torment of Hailfire, and Awaken the Woods. So, we saw the commander. What does the rest of the deck look like? Haddock Teague is usually best paired with a "hate bears" deck. "Hate bear" is usually a 2/2 creature for two mana with a static ability that negatively affects the game. Although it's not a 2/2, Thalia, Guardian of Thraben is probably the most famous "hate bear." Her powerful static ability slows control decks down a full turn, and—perhaps my favorite even makes spells cost one more. So if your opponent has completely run out of mana to play Etali, Primal Conqueror , if they have non-creature spells in their hand, they won't be able to cast any of them. To Thalia, it is worth adding her counterpart, Thalia, Heretic Cathar, which again helps slow down the game by forcing non-basic lands and opponents' creatures to enter the field flipped. There 's also Aven Mindcensor and Leonin Arbiter to prevent players from effectively searching their libraries for cards. Drannith Magistrate simply stops the play of commanders from the commander zone, as well as stopping a number of other mechanics. Containment Priest token creation and reanimation, and Collector Ouphe completely disables treasures and many other artifacts. Typically, creature-based decks like this are vulnerable to table sweeps, but thanks to Haddock, you're unlikely to see them. Of course, point deletion can still come in handy. Fortunately, the green and white colors do a great job of defense. Mother of Runes and Giver of Runes are great creature-based defenses, and cards like Heroic Intervention, Veil of Summer, Tamiyo's Safekeeping, and Teferi's Protection will help with everything else. To always have protection spells in hand, add draft cards to your deck . Beast Whisperer, Elemental Bond, and Oran, Frostfang can help with this. And to win the game, Beastmaster's Ascension, Moonshaker Cavalry, and Craterhoof Behemoth will turn your " hate-bears" into a deadly threat. One rule: reducing the cost does not bypass the Haddock effect. If Haddock is in play with seven other creatures, you cannot cast Blasphemous Act. Haddock simply looks at the mana cost in the upper right corner of the card. The same goes for cards that allow you spells without paying their mana cost. If the mana cost is four or more and it's not a creature , Haddock blocks it. Moving on to our next evil commander—Sen Triplets. Sen Triplets is a 3/3 Esper creature for five mana that says "At the beginning of your upkeep, choose target opponent." This turn, this player cannot spells or activate abilities , and their hand is open . You can play lands and spells from that player's hand during your turn. Being able to steal someone's combo or use their own removal against their own creatures is satisfying. And as a nice bonus, you also get the effect of a point-based Grand Abolisher. There are a few different ways to build a deck on Sen Triplets. Personally, I have an Esper Stax deck, but for this video we will focus on the topic of playing with opponent cards. It's worth noting: unlike Xanathar's ability, Sen Triplets' ability doesn't repair your mana. So you need to choose opponents with colors or mana fixers like Celestial Dawn, Mycosynth Lattice, Chromatic Lantern, or Chromatic Orrery . A couple more must-have cards for this deck are Telepathy and Paradox Haze. For just one blue mana, Telepathy lets you see all your opponents' hands to know who to target with Sen Triplets, and Paradox Haze is a three-mana spell that gives you extra upkeep. So with Sen Triplets in the game, you can choose two players for your turn. On this topic, many will recommend the Sphinx of the Second Sun, but it is one of the cards that is least understood correctly. You do not get a " start step" phase at the start of your main phase after combat. You get it after completing the main phase after the battle. So, while the card flip and card draw step are great, Sen Triplets doesn't use this card to its full potential. It's better to play Sakashima of a Thousand Faces or Sakashima the Imposter to simply copy Sen Triplets and get the extra effect that way. Thanks to D&D sets, we got a bunch of cards that provide support. Elder Brain and Brainstealer Dragon are two seven-mana 6/6s that each steal a lot of cards from your opponent and lock up mana so you can cast those spells. What I like most about these cards is that even if a creature dies, you can still play the cards they banished later. Next comes the Rogue's Class, which turns all your creatures into little Nightveil Specters. As you reach second level, your creatures become harder to block, which means you will activate the first ability more often. And at level three, you harvest and profit from all those stolen cards. This card requires a significant investment of mana, but the rewards can be huge. And of course, if we're talking about card stealing, we can't forget about Opposition Agent, a 3/2 three-man creature with Flash that opponents while they search their deck for something. And anything they find—under your control, of course— you can banish and play later if you want. Opposition Agent is great for hindering players trying to build combos. Search effects (Tutor) are everywhere now. So if you have a spare one, put it in this deck. This deck can use up mana quickly, so I highly set of Signets or Talismans, as well as cards like Thran Dynamo and Gilded Lotus. Of course, since we're playing evil decks, don't forget to include Smothering Tithe. Oh, and since we're playing blue, don't forget about counterspells and Diplomatic Immunity. Our next evil commander is Nevinar, the Urborg Tyrant. Nevinar is a 3/6 six-mana Esper zombie that has "Hexproof from artifacts, creatures, and spells." When Nevinar, Urborg Tyrant enters the battlefield, create a 2/2 black zombie token for each creature that died this turn. When Nevinar dies, you may pay a unit. When you do, destroy all artifacts, creatures, and spells. The game plan for this deck is simple. So , once we take out a commander, we play him again, because the deck is filled with all possible " doesn't die after all" effects.
